strengths: Timely and practically important problem: improving training efficiency for increasingly fine-grained and sparse MoE models is highly relevant to current large-scale AI systems.

The paper combines a clear systems insight with concrete implementation contributions: reduced activation caching, gather/epilogue fusion, IO/computation overlap, optimized top-k, and tile-aware token rounding.

The evaluation is broad for a kernel/system paper, covering activation memory and forward/backward throughput across multiple model-scale configurations, plus comparisons to ScatterMoE, MoMoE, MegaBlocks, Megatron, and DeepGEMM-based implementations.

The reported gains are substantial: lower per-layer activation memory, large kernel-level speedups, and an end-to-end 7B MoE training result showing similar throughput on 64 H100s to a baseline on 96 H100s.

The token rounding idea is simple, hardware-aware, and supported by both throughput measurements and language-model quality experiments, including ablations over rounding variants, microbatch size, and tile size.
The paper is generally well structured, technically detailed, and includes useful appendices with algorithms, benchmark configurations, and implementation-level comparisons.
weaknesses: The strongest empirical evidence is almost entirely on H100; although the method is described as tailored to Hopper and Blackwell, Blackwell support appears mostly design-level and not backed by comparable measured results.

The end-to-end training evaluation is limited: only one 7B-scale distributed training comparison is reported, while most results are single-layer or kernel-level. Communication-heavy expert parallel settings are explicitly left for future work, which limits claims about full large-scale MoE training.

The routing-quality evaluation for token rounding is still relatively small compared with frontier MoE claims: experiments are up to about 1.8B parameters and use modest token budgets, so the evidence for quality preservation at very large sparse MoE scale is suggestive rather than conclusive.

Some baseline comparisons depend on custom hybrid baselines such as DeepGEMM++ using the authors' optimized auxiliary kernels, which is reasonable but makes reproducibility and strict apples-to-apples interpretation harder.
The paper claims open-sourcing, but the manuscript text shows an empty GitHub link in the extracted PDF; if this is not just anonymization, it is a reproducibility weakness for a systems submission.
The scope is specialized to BF16 MoE kernels and particular NVIDIA GPU generations; broader precision formats, older GPUs, and non-NVIDIA hardware are not evaluated.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely bottleneck in MoE training: fine-grained and sparse MoEs increasingly shift cost from FLOPs to IO, padding, routing, and activation memory. The problem framing is relevant to modern large-scale AI systems.

The core systems ideas are technically plausible and useful: avoiding activation caching that scales with expert granularity, fusing gather/activation/gradient computations, overlapping IO with MMA, and tile-aware token rounding are all well motivated.

The kernel-level evaluation is broad, with comparisons against ScatterMoE, MoMoE, MegaBlocks, Megatron, DeepGEMM variants, and cuBLAS-style upper bounds across multiple model scales and MoE configurations.
The paper includes several helpful ablations, especially for token rounding variants, microbatch size, tile size, expert granularity, and kernel subcomponents.
The work could be practically useful if the implementation is robust and released as claimed, since the reported memory reductions and throughput gains are substantial in some configurations.
weaknesses: The main evidence is dominated by single-layer and kernel-level benchmarks. The end-to-end distributed training evidence is limited to one 7B setting, and the paper does not convincingly show how the approach behaves under realistic expert parallelism, all-to-all communication, pipeline interactions, optimizer overheads, or longer full-model training runs.

The token rounding quality evaluation is relatively weak for the strength of the claims. It is tested only at small-to-moderate pretraining scales with noisy downstream averages, no variance, and no strong evidence on larger models, instruction-tuned models, long-context settings, autoregressive generation quality, or real deployment inference behavior.

Some comparisons may favor the proposed system because baselines are combined with authors' optimized wrappers or are missing equivalent engineering effort. For example, DeepGEMM++ and other baselines are not necessarily complete mature MoE training stacks, and several failure/NA cases are not deeply analyzed.

Novelty is somewhat mixed. Many components are careful engineering combinations of known systems ideas such as gather fusion, epilogue fusion, ping-pong scheduling, activation recomputation/avoidance, and padding-aware routing. The paper would benefit from clearer separation between genuinely new algorithmic contributions and implementation-level optimization.

The reproducibility story is concerning: the text says the GitHub link is released but the manuscript appears to omit the actual link, and many claims depend on highly specialized CuTe-DSL kernels, hardware-specific scheduling, exact benchmark setup, and unpublished implementation details.

The top-K kernel uses packing of column indices into lower FP32 mantissa bits and assumes this does not affect sorting materially. This is a potentially delicate numerical/correctness issue, but the paper does not provide enough empirical error analysis or safeguards for close router logits.

The model-quality results often show very small differences between routing methods, sometimes within expected noise, yet the paper phrases quality preservation strongly. Lack of multiple seeds or confidence intervals makes several conclusions under-supported.

The paper is overly long and dense, with many claims scattered across appendices, future-model configurations, and low-level implementation details. This hurts clarity and makes it difficult to assess which results are central and independently reproducible.

Ethical and practical limitations are under-discussed. The work targets expensive frontier-scale GPU training and could increase compute demand; the paper does not discuss energy use, accessibility, or possible concentration-of-resources implications.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely bottleneck in fine-grained and sparse MoE training: activation memory, irregular IO, and padding waste increasingly dominate as MoE architectures scale toward more experts and smaller experts.

The technical contribution is substantive. The memory-efficient backward formulation avoids caching large O(TKd) activations while preserving the MoE computation, and the kernel design combines gather fusion, epilogue fusion, and MMA/IO overlap in a way that is well motivated by the hardware execution model.

The evaluation is strong for a systems paper: the authors compare against multiple relevant MoE implementations, include forward/backward kernel breakdowns, activation-memory measurements, model-scale configurations up to 120B-style and frontier-like MoE shapes, and an end-to-end FSDP-2 training throughput result on H100s.

The proposed token-rounding routing is a neat hardware-aware algorithmic contribution. It directly addresses grouped-GEMM tile quantization, has a simple bounded-deviation interpretation relative to token-choice routing, and is evaluated both for throughput and model quality.

The appendices are unusually useful: they include implementation comparisons, derivations, kernel ablations, top-K benchmarking, routing ablations, microbatch/tile sensitivity, and training hyperparameters, which improves confidence in the claims.

The reported gains are practically meaningful: reduced activation memory, large kernel speedups over strong baselines, and comparable 7B training throughput using substantially fewer H100s than ScatterMoE are all significant outcomes for MoE training practitioners.
weaknesses: The strongest empirical claims are highly hardware-specific, mainly centered on NVIDIA Hopper/Blackwell features and H100 benchmarking. This is appropriate for the contribution, but it limits generality and makes the impact dependent on adoption of these GPU generations and the authors' low-level implementation quality.

The token-rounding model-quality evaluation is relatively small compared with the systems scale of the paper: routing quality is tested around 0.5B-1.8B models and 20B-100B tokens, while the largest-system claims are kernel-level or configuration-level rather than full large-model training runs.

The end-to-end distributed training evidence is narrower than the kernel evaluation. The paper reports an important 7B/FSDP-2 throughput comparison, but does not fully study expert parallelism, all-to-all communication, communication/computation overlap, or multi-node behavior for the largest sparse MoE settings where these issues often dominate.

Some comparisons are difficult to interpret because several baselines require author-provided optimized wrappers or fail on some configurations. The authors discuss this, but the resulting comparison partly measures integration effort and feature coverage in addition to intrinsic kernel quality.

The paper makes strong claims about maintaining downstream quality with token rounding, but the downstream tasks are mostly standard small/medium LM benchmarks and single-run tables; uncertainty estimates, multiple seeds, and larger-scale downstream validation would make the quality-preservation claim more convincing.

Reproducibility depends on the promised open-source kernels and specialized CUDA/CuTe-DSL infrastructure. The manuscript says the kernels will be open-sourced, but the anonymized text leaves the repository link incomplete, so artifact availability cannot be verified from the submitted PDF.

strengths: Timely and practically important systems contribution for fine-grained and sparse MoE training, targeting a real bottleneck as modern MoE models move toward higher expert granularity and sparsity.

The paper presents a coherent co-design: activation-memory reduction via an equivalent backward computation, IO-aware fused grouped-GEMM kernels, Hopper/Blackwell-specific overlap strategies, an efficient top-K kernel, and tile-aware token rounding.

Evaluation is broad for a systems paper: comparisons include ScatterMoE, MoMoE, MegaBlocks, Megatron, DeepGEMM-based baselines, H100 and B300 results, multiple model-scale configurations, runtime breakdowns, activation-memory measurements, and several kernel ablations.

Reported gains are substantial and credible in direction: up to 45% activation memory reduction for a 7B fine-grained MoE, large forward/backward TFLOPS improvements, and an end-to-end 64-H100 vs 96-H100 training-throughput comparison.

The token rounding idea is simple, hardware-aware, and well motivated by tile quantization effects. The paper evaluates both throughput and model quality, including comparisons to token-choice, expert-choice, token dropping, and ablations over rounding strategy, microbatch size, and tile size.

The manuscript is technically detailed, with useful algorithmic descriptions, derivations of memory/IO costs, implementation-level discussion of Hopper and Blackwell scheduling, and appendices that materially support the main claims.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is weaker than claimed: the paper says the kernels are open-sourced but the GitHub link is blank in the manuscript. For a systems paper whose claims depend heavily on low-level implementation, this is a significant issue.

Most throughput evidence is single-layer/kernel-level. There is only one reported end-to-end distributed training throughput result, and the paper does not sufficiently evaluate interaction with expert parallelism, all-to-all communication, optimizer/state sharding, or full training at larger scales.

The strongest token rounding quality claims are based on relatively small language models and modest token budgets. Evidence that it preserves quality for frontier-scale sparse MoEs, long-context generation, downstream generative behavior, or post-training/instruction-tuned settings is limited.

Some baselines are necessarily customized or partially reconstructed, especially DeepGEMM++ and DeepGEMM-pt. While the authors explain these choices, the comparison depends on implementation assumptions that would benefit from independent reproducibility or more standardized benchmark harnesses.

The routing method changes training-time routing and is then evaluated by switching back to token-choice routing; this train-test mismatch is empirically explored but not theoretically characterized beyond bounded per-expert deviation. Cases where average tokens per expert approach one tile show degradation, suggesting nontrivial limits.

Several contributions are adaptations or combinations of known GPU optimization ideas, such as gather/epilogue fusion and ping-pong scheduling, applied carefully to MoE. The novelty is strong at the system integration level but less so for some individual kernel techniques.

The paper does not discuss broader usability constraints in depth, such as portability beyond recent NVIDIA architectures, integration complexity for existing training stacks, numerical stability/determinism tradeoffs, or support for FP8/MX formats, which are left mostly as future work.

strengths: Targets an important and timely bottleneck: efficient training of fine-grained and sparse MoE models, where activation memory, gather/scatter IO, and grouped-GEMM padding are practical limitations.
The paper presents a coherent set of systems techniques, including reduced activation caching, fused gather/epilogue operations, IO-overlapped grouped GEMM, and tile-aware token rounding.

The kernel-level evaluation is broad across model-shaped configurations, H100/B300 hardware, and several relevant MoE implementations, and the reported speedups and memory reductions are potentially useful if reproducible.
The token-rounding idea is simple, hardware-aware, and accompanied by several ablations over rounding strategy, microbatch size, and tile size.
weaknesses: The central evidence is dominated by kernel microbenchmarks. End-to-end training evidence is thin: the main real training throughput comparison uses different GPU counts, and token rounding speedups are mostly reported at the kernel/runtime level rather than as full distributed training improvements.

Reproducibility is a serious concern. The paper claims open sourcing, but the GitHub link is blank in the manuscript, and many results depend on highly specialized custom kernels, hardware, compiler behavior, and baseline modifications that are hard to verify from the paper alone.

Several comparisons are difficult to interpret. Some baselines are marked NA or fail on large configurations, while others are augmented with author-provided optimized components such as DeepGEMM++; this makes the fairness and practical meaning of the headline speedups less clear.

The token-rounding quality evaluation is too limited for the strength of the claims. It is tested only at relatively small language-model scales, with noisy downstream averages, no statistical uncertainty, and evaluation switches back to token-choice routing because TR itself is not directly autoregressive-friendly.

The paper claims no quality loss, but the tables show mixed behavior: token dropping sometimes matches or exceeds TR on downstream average, TR gains are small relative to benchmark noise, and degradation appears when the average expert token count approaches the tile size.

The novelty is partly incremental from a top-tier AI perspective: many contributions are engineering combinations of known systems ideas such as gather fusion, epilogue fusion, persistent scheduling, and activation-memory tradeoffs. The paper does not clearly separate what is algorithmically new from what is implementation craftsmanship.

Important practical settings are underexplored, including expert parallelism/all-to-all communication, FP8 or lower precision training, optimizer/state memory, numerical equivalence and stability, determinism, and integration cost in real training stacks.
The presentation is overly long and promotional, with many strong claims not matched by equally strong experimental controls. A clearer limitations section is also missing.

strengths: Timely and practically important problem: improving training efficiency for increasingly fine-grained and sparse MoE models on modern NVIDIA GPUs.
Technically strong contribution combining activation-memory analysis, mathematically equivalent backward computation avoiding cached Y/dY, IO-aware grouped GEMM kernels, and tile-aware routing.

Evaluation is broad for a systems paper: comparisons against ScatterMoE, MoMoE, MegaBlocks, Megatron, DeepGEMM variants, and Triton examples across H100 and B300, with memory, kernel throughput, layer throughput, and limited end-to-end training throughput.
Reported gains are substantial: lower activation memory, large forward/backward speedups over strong baselines, and a compelling 64-H100 vs 96-H100 training-throughput comparison.
The token rounding idea is simple, hardware-motivated, and accompanied by quality checks, routing baselines, and ablations over rounding subroutines, microbatch size, and tile size.
The paper is generally well organized, with clear algorithms, useful runtime breakdowns, and appendices that clarify gradient equivalence and benchmark configurations.
weaknesses: The claimed open-source release is undermined by a missing/blank GitHub link in the manuscript, which weakens reproducibility for a paper whose contribution depends heavily on low-level kernel details.

The strongest quality claims for token rounding are validated only at relatively small language-model scales and token budgets compared with the large MoE systems motivating the paper; it remains uncertain whether the train/evaluation routing mismatch is harmless at frontier scale or on generation-heavy evaluations.

Much of the main evidence is single-layer or kernel-level benchmarking. The paper includes one useful end-to-end FSDP result, but does not fully evaluate distributed MoE settings with expert parallelism/all-to-all communication, where practical bottlenecks may differ.

Several baselines require substantial adaptation or are reported as failing/OOM in some settings; while plausible, the paper would benefit from more detail on baseline tuning, versioning, and whether failures reflect inherent limitations or implementation choices.
The scope is mostly BF16 Hopper/Blackwell training. Low-precision formats, inference implications, and non-NVIDIA portability are deferred, limiting the generality of the contribution.
Some claims are phrased broadly, such as preserving quality without loss, while the evidence is more nuanced and conditional on microbatch/tile regimes and small-scale evaluations.
